Whoever among both is a believer is a friend of God, and whoever among both is a disbeliever is a devil.

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas that the jinn are the offspring of the jann, and they are not devils, and they die. Among them are believers and disbelievers. The devils are the offspring of Iblis, and they do not die except together with Iblis, their origin. Whoever claims that they are from the jann and not from the offspring of Iblis says that they will enter Paradise by their faith. Whoever says that they are from the offspring of Iblis has two opinions concerning them:

The first: they will enter it. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second, which is the narration of Mujahid: they will not enter it, even if they are turned away from the Fire.

Concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, there are three aspects:

The first: wondrous in the eloquence of its speech.

The second: wondrous in the eloquence of its admonitions.

The third: wondrous in the greatness of its blessing.

﴿It guides to right conduct﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects:

The first: the right paths of affairs.

The second: to the knowledge of God.

﴿And that He, the Exalted, is the majesty of our Lord﴾. Concerning this there are ten interpretations:

The first: the command of our Lord, said by al-Suddi.

The second: the act of our Lord, said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: the remembrance of our Lord, which is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: the wealth of our Lord, said by Ikrima.

The fifth: the trial of our Lord, said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: the dominion and authority of our Lord, said by Abu Ubayda.

The seventh: the majesty and greatness of our Lord, said by Qatada.

The eighth: the blessings of our Lord upon His creation, related by al-Dahhak.

The ninth: "exalted is the majesty of our Lord," meaning "exalted is our Lord," said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The tenth: they meant by "jadd" the grandfather, the father's father, and this would be a statement of the jinn out of [ignorance].

﴿And that our foolish one used to speak against God an excessive lie﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: our ignorant one, meaning the disobedient among us. Qatada said: The foolish one among the jinn disobeyed Him just as the foolish one among mankind disobeyed Him.

The second: that he is Iblis, said by Mujahid and Qatada, and related by Abu Burda ibn Abi Musa al-Ash'ari from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Concerning the word "shatatan" (excessive) there are two aspects:

The first: injustice, which is the view of Abu Malik.

The second: falsehood, said by al-Kalbi. The root of *shatat* is distance, so it is used to express injustice because of its distance from justice, and falsehood because of its distance from truth.

﴿And that there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾. Ibn Zayd said: In the pre-Islamic period, a man, when he descended into a valley, would say: "I seek refuge with the greatest of this valley," meaning from the jinn, "from the foolish ones of his people." When Islam came, they sought refuge in God and abandoned them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And that there were men﴾. Concerning His saying: ﴿So they increased them in *rahaq*﴾ there are eight interpretations:

The first: transgression, said by Mujahid.

The second: sin, said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. Al-A'sha said:

*Nothing benefits me except seeing her; can a lover be healed if he has not been struck by rahaq?*

Meaning: sin.

The third: fear, said by Abu al-Aliya, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: disbelief, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: harm, said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: error, said by Muqatil.

The seventh: pride, said by al-Kalbi.

The eighth: foolishness, related by Ibn Isa.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 72, verses 8–10:

﴿And that we touched the heaven﴾ has two interpretations:

One: "We sought the heaven," for the Arabs use touching (lams) to express seeking. They say: "I came seeking (almis) provision, and I sought (iltamis) provision."

The second: "We approached the heaven," for that which is touched is near.

﴿And we found it﴾ meaning its paths.(p-112)

﴿filled with strong guards﴾: these are the harsh, stern angels.

﴿and meteors﴾, plural of shihab (shihab), which is the falling of burning stars upon them when they eavesdrop. The scholars differed over whether such falling occurred in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period), before the mission of the Messenger ﷺ, into two opinions:

One: that they did fall in the Jahiliyyah, and that their increase at the mission of the Messenger was a warning concerning his condition. Aws ibn Hajar, who was a pre-Islamic poet, said:

؎ He swooped like a shooting star, followed by a rising cloud of dust, which you think to be a tent-rope.

This is the view of the majority.

The second: that the swooping did not occur before the mission, but that Allah brought it into being after it. Al-Jahiz said: "Every poem that is narrated about it is fabricated."

﴿And that we used to sit in some of its seats to listen﴾: meaning that the rebellious jinn used to sit in the lowest heaven in seats for listening, hearing the news of the heaven from the angels, until they conveyed it to the soothsayers, and it would flow on their tongues. So Allah guarded it when He sent His Messenger with the burning meteors. Then the jinn said at that time: ﴿Whoever listens now will find for himself a watching meteor (shihaban rasadan)﴾, meaning by the shihab the burning star, and by the rasad the angels [who watch].

As for the Revelation, the jinn were not able to hear it, for they had been prevented from it previously.

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance (rashad)﴾. Here there are two interpretations:

One: that they do not know whether Allah has sent Muhammad so that they may believe in him, and that will be guidance for them and a reward for them, or whether they will disbelieve in him, and that will be evil for them and punishment upon them. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij.

The second: that they do not know whether the guarding of the heaven with meteors is evil and punishment or guidance and reward. This was said by Ibn Zayd.(p-113)

(p-١١٤) Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 72, verses 11–17:

﴿And among us are the righteous﴾, meaning the believers.

﴿And among us are those short of that﴾, meaning the polytheists.

It is possible that by "the righteous" he means the people of goodness, and by "those short of that" the people of evil, and those between the two extremes in gradations. The interpretation that they refer to belief and polytheism is closer, because it is a report from them about the state they were in before their faith.

﴿We were divided into diverse ways﴾. On this there are three interpretations. The first: it means various factions. This is said by al-Suddi.

The second: various religions. This is said by al-Dahhak.

The third: divergent desires. From this is the verse of al-Ra'i:

*The one who grasps and extends, who guides by His obedience,*
*in the trial of people, when their desires are divided.*

﴿And when we heard the guidance, we believed in it﴾, meaning the Qur'an. They heard it from the Prophet (ﷺ), and they believed in it and affirmed his message. The Messenger of Allah had been sent to the jinn and to humankind.

al-Hasan said: Allah sent Muhammad to humankind and the jinn, and Allah did not send a messenger from among the jinn, nor from the people of the desert, nor from women. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾.

﴿Whoever believes in his Lord will fear neither diminution nor oppression﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he will not fear a reduction in his good deeds nor an increase in his bad deeds, because *al-bakhs* is reduction, and *al-rahaq* is transgression. This is a statement that Allah related about the jinn, due to the strength of their faith and the soundness of their submission. 'Ammar ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said:

"While 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was sitting one day, a man passed by him. It was said to him: 'Do you know the passer-by, Commander of the Believers?' He said: 'Who is he?' They said: 'Sawad ibn Qarib, a man from the people of Yemen who has standing, and he had a *ri'i* (companion) from the jinn.' 'Umar sent for him and said to him: 'Are you Sawad ibn Qarib?' He said: 'Yes, Commander of the Believers.' He said: 'And are you the one to whom a *ri'i* from the jinn came, appearing to you?' He said: 'Yes. One night, while I was between sleeping and waking, a *ri'i* from the jinn came to me, struck me with his foot, and said: "Get up, Sawad ibn Qarib, listen to my speech and understand, if you are able to understand. A messenger has been sent from Lu'ay ibn Ghalib, calling to Allah and to worshipping Him." Then he began to recite:

*I marvel at the jinn and their pursuit,*
*and their driving of camels by their tails.*

*They head toward Mecca seeking guidance;*
*the truthful among the jinn is not like its liars.*

*So set out to the elite of Hashim,*
*for no liar has come to them with it.*

(p-١١٥) I said: 'Leave me, for I have become drowsy,' and I did not lift my head to what he said. When the second night came, he came to me, struck me with his foot, and said: 'Get up, Sawad ibn Qarib, listen to my speech and understand, if you are able to understand. A messenger has been sent from Lu'ay ibn Ghalib, calling to Allah and to worshipping Him.' Then he began to recite:

*I marvel at the jinn and their choosing*
*and their driving of camels by their saddles.*

*They head toward Mecca seeking guidance;*
*the believer among the jinn is not like its disbelievers.*
*So set out to the elite of Hashim,*
*between its hills and its stones.*

I said to him: 'Leave me, for I have become drowsy,' and I did not lift my head to what he said. When the third night came, he came to me, struck me with his foot, and said: 'Get up, Sawad ibn Qarib, listen to my speech and understand, if you are able to understand. A messenger has been sent from Lu'ay ibn Ghalib, calling to Allah and to worshipping Him.' Then he began to recite:

*I marvel at the jinn and their scouting*
*and their driving of camels by their pack-saddles.*

*They head toward Mecca seeking guidance;*
*the best of the jinn is not like their filth.*
*So set out to the elite of Hashim,*
*and wipe with your hands over its head.*

He said: 'In the morning Allah had tested my heart with Islam, so I mounted my she-camel and came to Medina. There was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions. I said: "Listen to my speech, Messenger of Allah." He said: "Speak." So I began to say:

*A confidant came to me between stillness and sleep,*
*and what I recited was not a lie.*
*Three nights, his saying each night:*
*"A messenger from Lu'ay ibn Ghalib has come to you."*
*So I hitched up my garment and urged*
*the strong-legged camel between the desert plains.*
*I bear witness that Allah, there is none besides Him,*
*and that you are the one hoped for against every adversary.*

(p-١١٦)

*And that you are the closest of the messengers in intercession*
*to Allah, O son of the noblest and purest.*
*So command us with what comes to you, O best of those who walked,*
*even if in what came there is the whiteness of hair-locks.*
*And be my intercessor on a day when none has intercession*
*except you, to suffice against Sawad ibn Qarib.*"

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions rejoiced greatly, until the joy was seen in their faces. He said: 'Then 'Umar leapt up, embraced him, and said: "I have long wished to hear this account from you. Does your *ri'i* from the jinn come to you today?" He said: "[As for] now that I have recited the Qur'an, no. The Book of Allah is a fine replacement for the jinn."'"

﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the deviators﴾. This is a report of the jinn's speech about the state of those among them who are believers and disbelievers. *Al-qasit* means the one who oppresses, because he swerves from the truth. Its counterpart is *al-tirb* and *al-mutrab*. *Al-tirb* is the poor man, because the loss of his wealth made him sit on the dust (*al-turab*). *Al-mutrab* is the rich man, because the abundance of his wealth has become like dust.

Regarding the meaning of *al-qasitin* (the deviators) there are three aspects:

The first: the losers. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: the wicked. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: the covenant-breakers. This is said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And that if they had remained steadfast upon the way﴾. Ibn Bahr mentioned that every instance in this surah of *(inna)* with a kasra and doubled nun is a report of the speech of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an and returned to their people as warners, and every instance in it of *(anna)* with a fatha and either single or doubled nun is from the revelation to the Messenger.

Regarding this steadfastness there are two views:

The first: it is persistence upon the path of disbelief and misguidance. This is said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu Majlaz, and others.

The second: steadfastness upon guidance and obedience. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Qatadah, and Mujahid.

As for the one who holds that the meaning is persistence in disbelief and error, they have two views on His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾:

The first: We would test them with the abundance of plentiful water until they perish as the people of Noah perished by drowning. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The second: We would have given them abundant water, by which their crops would grow and their wealth would increase.

﴿So that We may test them therein﴾, meaning it would be an increase in trial. al-Suddi related from 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ that he said: "Wherever there is water there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth there is trial." So the trial here may have two meanings:

The first: the seduction of their own souls.

The second: the occurrence of trial and evil because of it.

As for the one who holds that the meaning is steadfastness upon guidance and obedience, they have four aspects regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾:

The first: its meaning is that We would have guided them to the straight path. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: We would have widened provision for them in this world. This is said by Qatadah.

The third: We would have given them a pleasant life. This is said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fourth: it is abundant wealth, due to the blessings upon them of the life of souls and the fertility of crops. This is said by Abu Malik, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd.

Regarding *al-ghadaq* (abundant) there are two views:

The first: that it is sweet, flowing water. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*Its mixture is Salsabil, its water is abundant,*
*sweet in taste, neither salty nor turbid.*

The second: that it is vast and plentiful. This is said by Mujahid, and from it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

*I gave Su'da its water and its vegetation;*
*not every lover gives to the one who loves him.*

*So that Su'da may be watered by it, and its neighborhood be watered,*
*and that the jars and drinking-places may overflow with it.*

(p-١١٨) Based on this, there are two aspects:

The first: that it is a report about their state in this world.

The second: that it is a report about their state in the Hereafter, "so that We may test them therein."

If it is said that this applies to the people of disbelief and error, then its interpretation has three aspects:

The first: the seduction of their own souls by the adornment of this world.

The second: the occurrence of trial and discord among them because of abundance of wealth.

The third: the occurrence of punishment upon them, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿The day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13], meaning they will be punished.

If it is said that it applies to the people of guidance and obedience, then it follows the two aspects we previously mentioned.

As for whether it is their testing in this world, then its interpretation has three aspects:

The first: that We may test them by it. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that We may purify them from the filth of disbelief.

The third: that We may bring them out by it from hardship and drought to abundance and fertility.

If it is said that it is a report about what is theirs in the Hereafter, then its interpretation has two aspects:

The first: that We may purify them and deliver them, derived from *fatana al-dhahab* (he tested the gold) when he purified it from its impurity by fire, as Allah, Exalted, said to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40], meaning We freed you from Pharaoh.

The second: its meaning is that We would turn them away from the Fire, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, to fabricate against Us other than it﴾ [al-Isra': 73], meaning they would turn you away.

﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord﴾. Ibn Zayd said: this means the Qur'an. Regarding his turning away from it, there are two aspects:

The first: from accepting it, if it is said that they are among the people of disbelief.

The second: from acting upon it, if it is said that they are among the believers.

﴿He will make him enter a punishment of ascending hardship﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: that it is a pit in the Fire. This is said by Abu Sa'id.

The second: a mountain in the Fire; when he places his hand upon it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns. This is reported, and these two aspects concern the punishment of the people of misguidance.

The third aspect: it is a hardship of punishment that rises upward (*yatasa'ad*). This is said by Mujahid.

*So set out to the elite of Hashim,*

*I marvel at the jinn and their choosing*
*and their driving of camels by their saddles.*

*They head toward Mecca seeking guidance;*
*the believer among the jinn is not like its disbelievers.*
*So set out to the elite of Hashim,*
*between its hills and its stones.*

*I marvel at the jinn and their scouting*
*and their driving of camels by their pack-saddles.*

*the best of the jinn is not like their filth.*
*So set out to the elite of Hashim,*

*A confidant came to me between stillness and sleep,*

*Three nights, his saying each night:*

*So I hitched up my garment and urged*

*to Allah, O son of the noblest and purest.*

The first: the losers. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: the wicked. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: the covenant-breakers. This is said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And that if they had remained steadfast upon the way﴾. Ibn Bahr mentioned that every instance in this surah of *(inna)* with a kasra and doubled nun is a report of the speech of the jinn who listened to the Qur'an and returned to their people as warners, and every instance in it of *(anna)* with a fatha and either single or doubled nun is from the revelation to the Messenger.

Regarding this steadfastness there are two views:

The first: it is persistence upon the path of disbelief and misguidance. This is said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu Majlaz, and others.

The second: steadfastness upon guidance and obedience. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Qatadah, and Mujahid.

As for the one who holds that the meaning is persistence in disbelief and error, they have two views on His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾:

The first: We would test them with the abundance of plentiful water until they perish as the people of Noah perished by drowning. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The second: We would have given them abundant water, by which their crops would grow and their wealth would increase.

﴿So that We may test them therein﴾, meaning it would be an increase in trial. al-Suddi related from 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ that he said: "Wherever there is water there is wealth, and wherever there is wealth there is trial." So the trial here may have two meanings:

The first: the seduction of their own souls.

The second: the occurrence of trial and evil because of it.

As for the one who holds that the meaning is steadfastness upon guidance and obedience, they have four aspects regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾:

The first: its meaning is that We would have guided them to the straight path. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: We would have widened provision for them in this world. This is said by Qatadah.

The third: We would have given them a pleasant life. This is said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fourth: it is abundant wealth, due to the blessings upon them of the life of souls and the fertility of crops. This is said by Abu Malik, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd.

Regarding *al-ghadaq* (abundant) there are two views:

The first: that it is sweet, flowing water. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*Its mixture is Salsabil, its water is abundant,*
*sweet in taste, neither salty nor turbid.*

The second: that it is vast and plentiful. This is said by Mujahid, and from it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

*I gave Su'da its water and its vegetation;*
*not every lover gives to the one who loves him.*

*So that Su'da may be watered by it, and its neighborhood be watered,*
*and that the jars and drinking-places may overflow with it.*

(p-١١٨) Based on this, there are two aspects:

The first: that it is a report about their state in this world.

The second: that it is a report about their state in the Hereafter, "so that We may test them therein."

If it is said that this applies to the people of disbelief and error, then its interpretation has three aspects:

The first: the seduction of their own souls by the adornment of this world.

The second: the occurrence of trial and discord among them because of abundance of wealth.

The third: the occurrence of punishment upon them, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿The day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13], meaning they will be punished.

If it is said that it applies to the people of guidance and obedience, then it follows the two aspects we previously mentioned.

As for whether it is their testing in this world, then its interpretation has three aspects:

The first: that We may test them by it. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that We may purify them from the filth of disbelief.

The third: that We may bring them out by it from hardship and drought to abundance and fertility.

If it is said that it is a report about what is theirs in the Hereafter, then its interpretation has two aspects:

The first: that We may purify them and deliver them, derived from *fatana al-dhahab* (he tested the gold) when he purified it from its impurity by fire, as Allah, Exalted, said to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40], meaning We freed you from Pharaoh.

The second: its meaning is that We would turn them away from the Fire, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, to fabricate against Us other than it﴾ [al-Isra': 73], meaning they would turn you away.

The first: from accepting it, if it is said that they are among the people of disbelief.

The second: from acting upon it, if it is said that they are among the believers.

﴿He will make him enter a punishment of ascending hardship﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: that it is a pit in the Fire. This is said by Abu Sa'id.

The second: a mountain in the Fire; when he places his hand upon it, it melts, and when he lifts it, it returns. This is reported, and these two aspects concern the punishment of the people of misguidance.

The third aspect: it is a hardship of punishment that rises upward (*yatasa'ad*). This is said by Mujahid.

﴿And the mosques are for Allah﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: it means the prayers are for Allah. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

The second: it means the limbs with which one prostrates are for Allah. This was said by al-Rabi'.

The third: it means the mosques, which are the houses of Allah for prayer. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it means every place where a person has prayed; because of prostration in it, it is called a masjid (mosque).

﴿So do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾, that is, do not worship anyone alongside Him. Regarding its occasion (sabab) there are three opinions. The first: what al-A'mash related, that the jinn said, "O Messenger of Allah, permit us to witness the prayer with you in your mosque," and so this verse was revealed.

The second: what Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali related, that the Humus, from the polytheists of Makkah, namely Kinana, 'Amir and Quraysh, used to recite the talbiyah around the House: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns." So Allah revealed this verse forbidding that He be given a partner.

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) entered the mosque, he would put forward his right foot and say: ﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾. O Allah, I am Your servant and Your visitor, and every visitor has a right, and You are the best of visitors. So I ask You, by Your mercy, to free my neck from the Fire." ﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). Regarding this there are two possibilities.

One: he stood to pray, calling upon his Lord within it, and his companions stood behind him following him, so the jinn marvelled at the obedience of his companions to him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: he stood up before the Jews, inviting them to Allah. This was narrated by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿They almost became a crowd upon him﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

The first: it means helpers. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it means groups, piled upon one another; this is the meaning of Mujahid's statement, and from it comes "labad" (a mass of wool piled upon one another). Dhu al-Rummah said:

"A watering place, stagnant, its waterings desolate, its stars green, from a clotted, matted mire."

Regarding their being "a crowd upon him," there are three possibilities.

One: they are the Muslims gathering around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: they are the jinn when they listened to the Messenger of Allah's recitation. This was said by al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam.

The third: they are the jinn and humans cooperating against the Messenger of Allah in polytheism. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿Say: I have no power to harm you or to bring you right guidance﴾, meaning harm to those who believe, and no right guidance for those who disbelieve. Regarding this there are three possibilities:

One: punishment and no bounty.

The second: death and no life.

The third: misguidance and no guidance.

﴿Say: none will protect me from Allah, and I shall not find any refuge other than Him﴾. Abu al-Jawza related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I set out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the jinn until he reached al-Hajun. He drew a line, then advanced over them, and they crowded around him. A chief of theirs called Wardan said: 'I will drive them away from you.' He said: (None will protect me from Allah)." It may bear two meanings:

One: none will protect me, alongside Allah's protection of me.

The second: none will protect me from what Allah has decreed for me.

﴿And I shall not find any refuge other than Him﴾. Regarding this there are three possibilities:

One: it means a refuge or a shelter. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: a protector or a patron. This was narrated by Abu Sa'id.

The third: a path or a way. This was related by Ibn Shajara, and from it is the statement of the poet:

"Alas for my soul, and alas, unavailing, from me, and there is no escape from Allah's decree."

﴿Except a message from Allah and His messages﴾. Regarding this there are two possibilities:

One: I have no power to harm or to guide you, except that I convey the messages of Allah. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: none will protect me from Allah if I do not convey the messages of Allah. This was said by Muqatil.

Makhul related from Ibn Mas'ud: "The jinn pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on this night, and they were seventy thousand, and they finished their pledge at the breaking of dawn."

Second: what you do not see of what is hidden from you. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Third: the unseen is the Qur'an. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: the unseen is the Resurrection and what happens in it. Ibn Abi Hatim related this view.

First: "except to a messenger whom He has approved" refers to Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

First: the guard (rasad) is the path. Its meaning is that He makes for him a path to knowledge of some of what came before and what will come after. This is the view of Ibn Bahr.
